notes: Actual results for the fiscal year ended November 30, 2024, as the county reported them in its Annual Financial Report to the Illinois Comptroller. Not a budget.

Public schools are run by separate school districts with their own taxes, so they are not included. The county collector gathers property taxes for every taxing district and pays them over; that money is left out.

Covers the general, special revenue, capital projects, debt service and enterprise (utility) funds. Pension trusts and other fiduciary funds, internal service funds and component units are left out, as are transfers between funds and borrowing.
Depreciation ($39,757) is left out; capital outlay is counted when paid.
Capital outlay outside utility funds ($3,681,182) is reported without a function, so it is spread over the county's services in proportion to their spending.
Courts, legal services, public buildings, housing and community development count as overhead.
Debt is bonds, contracts and other long-term debt outstanding at year end (beginning balance plus new debt less debt retired), as reported.

Political money counts contributions from businesses, unions and PACs to county board and county office candidates, reported to the State Board of Elections since 2023. Illinois allows business contributions. Individuals, candidates' own money, party and candidate committees, loans and other receipts are not counted.
Transparency practices have not been checked yet, so they are not scored.

Red flags: surveillance programs come from the EFF Atlas of Surveillance, a public database of news reports and public records, searched on 2026-10-14. A town or county with none listed may still have programs nobody has reported. Data center deals, corporate tax breaks and license-plate cameras mapped by volunteers have not been checked for Illinois yet. Most records carry no dollar amount, so each documented program costs a quarter of the red-flag points instead of being counted as spending.

redFlags.label: Police drones
redFlags.detail: The Macon County Sheriff's Office has four drones, according to the 2024 Illinois Freedom from Drone Surveillance Act Report. The agency conducted two drone flights between July 2023 and March 2024.

notes: Actual results for the fiscal year ended April 30, 2024, as the village reported them in its Annual Financial Report to the Illinois Comptroller. Not a budget.

Public schools are run by separate school districts with their own taxes, so they are not included. Residents also pay Macon County and, in most counties, the township they live in; park, library and fire protection districts are separate governments too.

Covers the general, special revenue, capital projects, debt service and enterprise (utility) funds. Pension trusts and other fiduciary funds, internal service funds and component units are left out, as are transfers between funds and borrowing.
Depreciation ($58,059) is left out; capital outlay is counted when paid.
Courts, legal services, public buildings, housing and community development count as overhead.
Debt is bonds, contracts and other long-term debt outstanding at year end (beginning balance plus new debt less debt retired), as reported.

Political money is not scored: no candidates for mayor or village president, council or board, clerk and other local offices of Village of Warrensburg reported contributions to the State Board of Elections since 2023.
Transparency practices have not been checked yet, so they are not scored.

Red flags: surveillance programs come from the EFF Atlas of Surveillance, a public database of news reports and public records, searched on 2026-10-14. A town or county with none listed may still have programs nobody has reported. Data center deals, corporate tax breaks and license-plate cameras mapped by volunteers have not been checked for Illinois yet. Most records carry no dollar amount, so each documented program costs a quarter of the red-flag points instead of being counted as spending.

Public schools are run by separate school districts with their own taxes, so they are not included. Residents also pay Macon County; park, library and fire protection districts are separate governments too.
Illinois townships maintain township roads, assess property and provide general assistance; most also cover the cities and villages inside them.

Covers the general, special revenue, capital projects, debt service and enterprise (utility) funds. Pension trusts and other fiduciary funds, internal service funds and component units are left out, as are transfers between funds and borrowing.
Capital outlay outside utility funds ($10,000) is reported without a function, so it is spread over the township's services in proportion to their spending.
Courts, legal services, public buildings, housing and community development count as overhead.
Debt is bonds, contracts and other long-term debt outstanding at year end (beginning balance plus new debt less debt retired), as reported.

Political money is not scored: no candidates for mayor or village president, council or board, clerk and other local offices of South Macon Township reported contributions to the State Board of Elections since 2023.
Transparency practices have not been checked yet, so they are not scored.

Red flags: surveillance programs come from the EFF Atlas of Surveillance, a public database of news reports and public records, searched on 2026-10-14. A town or county with none listed may still have programs nobody has reported. Data center deals, corporate tax breaks and license-plate cameras mapped by volunteers have not been checked for Illinois yet. Most records carry no dollar amount, so each documented program costs a quarter of the red-flag points instead of being counted as spending.
